prompt:
Research what the Python Software Foundation or the CPython developers have officially said about the performance impact of the free-threaded (no-GIL) build. Cite the PEP or documentation page and quote the relevant statement.

Output format (required):
For every claim you attribute to a source, write one line in exactly this form:
SOURCE: <full URL> | QUOTE: "<a sentence copied word-for-word from that page>" | CLAIM: <what you take it to show>
For anything the task asks about that you could not find a source for, write one line:
NO_SOURCE_FOUND: <what you could not find>
You can write normal explanation before or after these lines.

response.content:
Here are the official statements from CPython developers and the Python Software Foundation regarding the performance impact of the free-threaded (no-GIL) build.

SOURCE: https://peps.python.org/pep-0703/ | QUOTE: "The changes to make CPython thread-safe without the GIL increase execution overhead for `--disable-gil` builds." | CLAIM: The free-threaded build incurs additional execution overhead compared to standard builds.
SOURCE: https://peps.python.org/pep-0703/ | QUOTE: "One thread | 6% | 5%" | CLAIM: Single-threaded code runs approximately 5-6% slower on x86_64 architectures (Intel Skylake and AMD Zen 3 respectively).
SOURCE: https://peps.python.org/pep-0703/ | QUOTE: "Multiple threads | 8% | 7%" | CLAIM: Multi-threaded code runs approximately 7-8% slower on x86_64 architectures, with the higher overhead partly due to bytecode specialization limits in threaded contexts.
SOURCE: https://peps.python.org/pep-0703/ | QUOTE: "However, with the GIL disabled, programs that use multiple threads should also be able to more effectively use multiple CPU cores." | CLAIM: Despite the execution overhead, free-threaded builds should achieve better overall throughput by utilizing multiple CPU cores in parallel.
SOURCE: https://peps.python.org/pep-0703/ | QUOTE: "Note that this PEP would not affect the performance of the default (non `--disable-gil`) builds of CPython." | CLAIM: Standard GIL-enabled builds are not impacted by these changes; the overhead is isolated to the free-threaded configuration.
SOURCE: https://peps.python.org/pep-0779/ | QUOTE: "the performance penalty on linear performance, comparing a free-threaded build against a with-GIL build, as measured by the pyperformance benchmarks (for example as run by Microsoft’s Faster CPython team, or Meta’s Python Runtime team), is currently around 10% (except on macOS, where it’s more like 3%)" | CLAIM: Current overhead is approximately 10% on Linux/Windows and 3% on macOS.
SOURCE: https://peps.python.org/pep-0779/ | QUOTE: "We propose a target of 20% (geometric mean, as measured by pyperformance) for phase II." | CLAIM: An increase in memory usage of up to 20% is considered acceptable for the free-threaded build to be officially supported.
SOURCE: https://peps.python.org/pep-0779/ | QUOTE: "Realistically, though, higher memory use is the cost of having efficient, safe free-threading, and we are unlikely to get this very close to the with-GIL build’s memory use without significant performance cost." | CLAIM: Elevated memory usage is an inherent trade-off of the free-threaded design and is not expected to reach parity with standard builds without sacrificing speed.
SOURCE: https://peps.python.org/pep-0779/ | QUOTE: "It’s not a simple drop-in solution – some code will have to be redesigned to make the most of the new capability, as well as avoid performance pitfalls – but it can achieve higher performance, significantly lower latency and new thread-based functionality when embraced." | CLAIM: Free-threading requires code redesign to avoid performance pitfalls, but offers higher throughput and lower latency when properly utilized.
SOURCE: https://docs.python.org/3/howto/free-threading-python.html | QUOTE: "On the pyperformance benchmark suite, the average overhead ranges from about 1% on macOS aarch64 to 8% on x86-64 Linux systems." | CLAIM: Official documentation reports single-threaded performance overhead between 1% (macOS ARM) and 8% (Linux x86_64).
SOURCE: https://docs.python.org/3/howto/free-threading-python.html | QUOTE: "The free-threaded build will typically use more memory compared to the default build." | CLAIM: Users should expect increased memory consumption when switching to the free-threaded build.
SOURCE: https://docs.python.org/3/howto/free-threading-python.html | QUOTE: "Free-threaded execution allows for full utilization of the available processing power by running threads in parallel on available CPU cores." | CLAIM: The free-threaded build enables true parallel execution of Python threads across multiple CPU cores.
